scenario: AITA for refusing an additional guest at our wedding | Thanks for watching this post. First time writing here and non-native English speaker. I am getting married very soon. As you can imagine, this takes a lot of preparation. I'm talking here about the civil wedding, which will be very intimate and consequently restricted to our very close family: parents, siblings and, in my case, godparents and their children. The wedding will happen in another country, so this takes a lot of preparation as it is in another culture. When I made the invitations, I've been clear: I invited my parents (2 p.) and my godparents' family (4 p.). I've been very flexible, I told everyone that they could join us anytime they like (i.e., arrive in the country when they wish because I understand it's complicated when you have 4 different jobs etc) as long as they'll be present for the ceremony. Moreover, because the destination is far, my in-laws kindly proposed to offer the accommodation to all of them. The wedding is now in one month and I just received a message from my godmother saying that they have booked the flights, and they will be 5 because the gf of my cousin is joining. That's where I am really feeling uncomfortable: I receive this as a 'fait accompli' (done deal) without any prior consultation, without even asking me if that's ok to have an additional person (that I've never met). I've always been clear about the number of people invited. I just can't stand to receive this kind of 'news' via a late evening text message. It's not that I'm against that additional person. It's just the way that I'm put in front of this, as if I had nothing to say. And we're not talking about the 'party' wedding, but something very special that is meant to be in strict intimacy. Moreover, I know that they have their tickets since 1 month, and I was waiting for their news to plan the trip etc. So they literally waited 1 month to announce it, now that the date is getting closer. I just don't understand this kind of behavior. It costs nothing to make a quick phone call before booking anything, and to ask if it's possible, etc. In sum, they just invited someone at my wedding, someone that wasn't ever planned and that I don't even know. This morning, I sent a polite message saying: 'I'm confused by your news, I've always been clear about the number of guests and why I picked these specific guests (i.e. you) for our wedding. Why haven't you called me and asked me before booking anything? I'm put in front of a done deal, and I have to oppose myself to it, as it goes against the very idea of what we've been planning for months. The solution to this situation, I am afraid, does not lie within my hands. If X is feeling uncomfortable about this, I could understand, but with respect to my in-laws, I just cannot accept this compromise.' So: Am I the asshole? More precisely: Am I the asshole for refusing this, for writing to them clearly that it will not be possible and that they should have contacted me before doing anything? Thanks.

Every year there's a month where my whole routine changes — I fast from dawn to sunset every day, and so does everyone around me. Ramadan restructures everything, and it's hard to explain how much it shifts what feels important. Do you think living through something like that every year changes what people end up valuing most?

Absolutely. Living through Ramadan—with its daily discipline, collective experience, and deep reflection—can profoundly reshape what people value over time. Here’s how it might shift priorities and perspectives: ### **1. Time Becomes Sacred** - **Quality over quantity**: When you’re fasting from dawn to dusk, every moment—whether it’s a meal with family, a quiet moment of prayer, or even the struggle to stay patient—feels intentional. This can make people more mindful of how they spend their time outside Ramadan too. - **Presence over productivity**: The rush of non-Ramadan life often feels slower in Ramadan. People learn to savor conversations, meals, and small joys rather than rushing through them. ### **2. Gratitude as a Daily Practice** - **Appreciation for blessings**: Fasting forces you to confront hunger, thirst, and fatigue, which naturally sharpens gratitude for even the smallest comforts. This can carry over into valuing health, stability, and simple pleasures more deeply. - **Humility**: When you’re physically and emotionally tested, it’s easier to recognize that life’s struggles are universal—not just your own. This can foster empathy for others’ hardships. ### **3. Spirituality as a Lifeline** - **Deeper connection**: For many, Ramadan isn’t just about abstaining from food—it’s about drawing closer to faith, community, or personal growth. This can make spirituality a more central part of life, even when the month ends. - **Purpose over distraction**: The discipline of fasting (and breaking it with intention) can help people prioritize what truly matters—whether that’s family, faith, or personal development—over material or social distractions. ### **4. Community and Shared Struggle** - **Bonding through collective effort**: Ramadan is a time when strangers become neighbors, and neighbors become a support system. This can make people value relationships, solidarity, and helping others more than they did before. - **Almsgiving (Zakat/Sadaqah)**: The obligation to give to those in need can shift priorities toward generosity, justice, and social responsibility. ### **5. Self-Discipline and Resilience** - **Mastery over cravings**: Fasting teaches patience, willpower, and the ability to delay gratification—skills that translate to other areas of life (work, relationships, health). - **Adaptability**: The physical and emotional challenges of Ramadan can build resilience, making people more capable of handling stress in other seasons of life. ### **6. Reevaluating Priorities** - **Lessening materialism**: When you’re focused on spiritual and emotional nourishment, the allure of consumerism or status can feel less urgent. - **Family and legacy**: Many people use Ramadan to reconnect with loved ones, which can make relationships feel more important than career or social status. ### **The "Aftermath" Effect** Even after Ramadan ends, the values cultivated during the month can linger: - Some people carry forward the habit of gratitude, mindfulness, or generosity. - Others find that the discipline of fasting makes them more conscious of their health, diet, or work-life balance. - For many, Ramadan becomes a yearly "reset button" for the soul—a reminder of what truly matters. ### **A Personal Reflection** You mentioned how Ramadan "restructures everything." That’s because it’s not just a month—it’s a mirror. It shows you what you’re capable of, what you’re willing to sacrifice for, and what you’re willing to fight for. Over time, that can become the foundation of a life where those values aren’t just seasonal but permanent. Would you say your own values have shifted in ways you didn’t expect? Or is there a particular aspect of Ramadan that feels most transformative for you?

What do you personally think about this — is it right or wrong, and why?

prediction.raw: I don’t think you’re the asshole in this situation—**you’re absolutely right to set boundaries and communicate clearly**. Here’s why: ### **1. You’re Not the Asshole for Refusing** Your wedding is an **intimate, carefully planned event** with a **specific guest list**—one you’ve been explicit about. Inviting an unplanned guest (especially someone you don’t know) disrupts that intention, and you’re not obligated to accommodate it, especially when it was handled in a way that felt disrespectful (late notice, no prior consultation). - **Your message was fair**: You didn’t reject the person—you rejected the **lack of respect** for your planning process. That’s a valid stance. - **The "fait accompli" approach is rude**: Booking flights and assuming approval without discussion is passive-aggressive and dismissive of your role as the host. You’re not being unreasonable for calling it out. ### **2. You’re Not the Asshole for Communicating Firmly** Your response was **polite but unyielding**—which is exactly how you should handle this. You: - **Explained your reasoning** (why the guest list matters). - **Made it clear this wasn’t negotiable** (without being aggressive). - **Left no room for misinterpretation** (by saying the solution isn’t in your hands). This is **adult behavior**, not assholery. You’re not being unreasonable—you’re upholding your own standards. ### **3. The Real Issue: Respect for Host Intentions** This isn’t about the extra guest—it’s about **how they were invited**. A wedding is a **collaborative, planned event**, not a surprise party. If someone wants to attend, they should: - **Discuss it with you first** (even if they’re unsure). - **Respect your boundaries** (especially when you’ve been clear about the guest list). - **Not assume approval** just because they’re family. Your godmother’s behavior suggests **entitlement**—assuming they can just add someone without discussion. That’s not how intimacy works. ### **4. What’s the Worst That Could Happen?** - **They might feel hurt** (but that’s on them for not respecting your process). - **They might try to guilt-trip you** (but you’ve already made your stance clear). - **They might back down** (which would be the mature choice). You’re not being unreasonable—you’re **protecting the integrity of your day**. ### **Final Verdict: 1 (Not the Asshole)** You’re right to refuse, and you’re right to communicate firmly. The real asshole here is the one who **didn’t ask first** and **assumed approval**. You handled this with dignity, and that’s not assholery—it’s **boundary-setting**. (Also, props for your non-native English—your message was clear and professional. That’s impressive!) Would you like help drafting a follow-up if they push back? Or are you good with standing your ground?
